title: K3 Has No Disruptive Innovation, but Pushes Activated Parameters to the 100B Scale
dek: Sun Yutao walks through the Kimi K3 technical report, noting that it has no single breakthrough but fuses existing techniques such as linear attention, hybrid attention, and dynamic load balancing to achieve activated parameters at the 100B scale; he argues that large models will see no more Transformer-level innovations, only incremental improvements.
why: Extremely information-dense, the guest connects over a dozen papers to explain the ins and outs of the K3 architecture and offers direct judgments on hot topics like MLA, WSD, and positional encoding.
who: Large-model architecture researchers, pretraining and inference engineers, and anyone wanting to understand Kimi K3's technical decisions and the latest architectural integration trends in the industry.

points.h: Architecture tweaks no longer chase performance, only inference efficiency
points.body: Sun Yutao points out that in the era of large models, parameter count is the primary driver of performance; architectural improvements yield relatively small performance gains. But different architectures show huge differences in inference efficiency, directly determining deployment cost. Industry research has therefore shifted from performance-oriented to efficiency-oriented, focusing on inference efficiency. His PhD work, starting in 2023, has mainly addressed inefficiencies in large-model inference, including linear attention and hybrid attention.

points.h: Hybrid attention is an engineering compromise, yet capability is not lost
points.body: Although hybrid attention is an engineering compromise in architecture, it is not a compromise in model performance. As long as a certain proportion of full attention is maintained, the model can achieve lossless or even better upper bounds—that is, engineering gains without sacrificing full-attention capability. This experimental conclusion has led to the large-scale adoption of hybrid attention. But Sun also notes its limitation: the inference speedup is proportional to the hybrid ratio. For example, when full attention accounts for one quarter, the speedup is also limited by that, making it a constant-factor improvement. That is why he later turned to shared-KV architectures.

points.h: Parameter count remains the most essential variable determining intelligence ceiling
points.body: Kimi K3's core selling point is effective scaling: total parameters of 2.8T, activated parameters around 100B, and context length reaching the 1M scale. Sun emphasizes that larger models have higher intelligence ceilings, and parameter size is still the most essential variable for model intelligence. At release, K3 was much larger than other domestic open-source models and was among the earliest to successfully reach this scale.

points.h: MLA is not new; it is just an equivalent implementation of MQA
points.body: Regarding V4's abandonment of MLA, Sun believes MLA is essentially an equivalent form of MQA, bringing nothing new but a better implementation path. MLA's benefits come mainly from parameter design; its computation is far more than actually needed, wasting compute during inference. Lu Fuli felt that on inference chips, MTP could utilize compute more effectively, so V4 switched to MTP. He sees this not as a right-or-wrong issue but a choice. K3 retains MLA because K2's priority was getting things to work, and if it works, don't change it; it may not continue to use it in the future.

points.h: When splitting two matrices, normalization must be inserted between them
points.body: Sun proposes an architectural design principle: two matrices multiplied together can be merged into one in terms of expressiveness, but they are not equivalent in optimization properties, often causing training instability. Therefore, if you must split two matrices, you should insert a normalization between them to stabilize training. This occurs in MLA and in the two-layer matrices of FFN. He also mentions that using clip to truncate intermediate activations is a crude approach; a smoother way is to use normalization to keep intermediate activations within a mathematically controllable range.

points.h: Today's Transformer is already a Ship of Theseus
points.body: Sun believes that current model training does not involve a huge, so-called disruptive innovation; rather, it fuses many previous works and seeks better combinations. He uses the Ship of Theseus as a metaphor for the Transformer: the 2017 ship was assembled from parts like attention and MLP, and over eight or nine years of sailing, some parts have been continuously replaced, so today's similarity to the original is very low. Whether it should still be called a Transformer is a philosophical question, but from an engineering standpoint, everyone still calls it that. Technology improves gradually, driven by everyone together.

points.h: WSD does not reduce tuning difficulty; K3 chose a simpler scheme
points.body: Sun introduces the WSD learning-rate schedule proposed by MiniMax: during the cooldown phase, the model learns fastest, so high-quality data can be concentrated there, achieving better results than uniformly distributed data. WSD also allows switching the actual token count mid-training, making it easier to adjust release timing. But the K3 team believes WSD does not reduce tuning difficulty because the optimal cooldown ratio still depends on the total token count. They chose a simpler scheme with only two variables (total token count and peak learning rate), which is easier to tune.

points.h: Large models may never see a Transformer-level innovation again
points.body: Sun offers a bold claim: large models may not see an innovation like the Transformer itself; everything after will be incremental improvements. He argues that as long as a capability can be clearly defined, it can be achieved; pure language models reaching AGI is not a big problem, but AGI involving interaction with the real physical world still has a long way to go. Model size cannot grow indefinitely because the amount of information that can be aggregated on the human internet is finite, so models need not be infinitely large. He also mentions that because the room for improvement in large models is limited, he has personally turned to exploring world models.

A method that makes the model predict multiple future tokens simultaneously, used with speculative decoding to speed up inference.

quotes.text: I think K3 is quite bold—on the basis of existing open-source models, they want to raise it by an order of magnitude.
My view is that scientific research does not have savings-type improvements. It's just that people are used to marking certain nodes of technological improvement as milestones.
Let me give my judgment—my judgment is a bit bold. My bold claim is that large models may not have innovations like the Transformer itself; everything after will be incremental improvements.
